Brief: Describe the Great Barrier Reef and the threats it faces. — about Geology and geography

1. 10 million years ago, the sea level significantly lowered, which further enabled sedimentation.
2. The reef's substrate may have needed to build up from the sediment until its edge was too far away for suspended sediments to inhibit coral growth.
3. In addition, approximately 400,000 years ago there was a particularly warm Interglacial period with higher sea levels and a 4 °C (7 °F) water temperature change.
4. The land that formed the substrate of the current Great Barrier Reef was a coastal plain formed from the eroded sediments of the Great Dividing Range with some larger hills (most of which were themselves remnants of older reefs or, in rare cases, volcanoes).
5. The Reef Research Centre, a Cooperative Research Centre, has found coral 'skeleton' deposits that date back half a million years.
6. The Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Authority (GBRMPA) considers the earliest evidence of complete reef structures to have been 600,000 years ago.
7. According to the GBRMPA, the current, living reef structure is believed to have begun growing on the older platform about 9,000 years ago.
8. The Australian Institute of Marine Science agrees, placing the beginning of the growth of the current reef at the time of the Last Glacial Maximum.
9. At around that time, sea level was 120 metres (390 ft) lower than it is today.
10. From 20,000 years ago until 6,000 years ago, sea level rose steadily around the world.
11. As it rose, the corals could then grow higher on the newly submerged maritime margins of the hills of the coastal plain.
12. By around 13,000 years ago the sea level was only 60 metres (200 ft) lower than the present day, and corals began to surround the hills of the coastal plain, which were, by then, continental islands.
